# Sasapaṇḍitajātaka (Ja 316)

**ID:** Ja 316
**Section:** Jātaka (ja)
**Collection:** Suttas-Late-1
**Title (Pali):** Sasapaṇḍitajātaka
**tipitaka.org (CST):** https://tipitaka.org/romn/cscd/s0513m.mul3.xml

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and catalog data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Sasapaṇḍitajātaka* (Ja 316), also known as the *Sasajātaka*, belongs to the *Catukkanipāta* of the Pali Jātaka collection [Buddhist Virtues 2011]. In the narrative framework of the "story of the present" (*paccuppannavatthu*), the Buddha relates the story while residing at Jetavana on the occasion of a landowner who provided meals to the Buddha and the monastic Saṅgha for seven consecutive days, culminating in an offering of all the monastic requisites [Ohnuma 2007]. In the "story of the past" (*atītavatthu*), the Bodhisatta is born as a wise hare dwelling in a forest with three animal companions: an otter, a jackal, and a monkey (identified in the identification of births with Ānanda, Moggallāna, and Sāriputta, respectively) [Nyanaponika et al. 2003; Ohnuma 2007]. After instructing his companions on keeping the observance day (*uposatha*) and practicing generosity, the god Sakka tests their commitment disguised as an impoverished, hungry brahmin [Nyanaponika et al. 2003; Ohnuma 2007]. While the other three animals gather ordinary food, the hare—having nothing else to give—resolves to offer his own body; he asks the brahmin to build a fire and leaps into the flames to provide roasted meat, but the fire magically remains cool and does not burn him [Nyanaponika et al. 2003; Ohnuma 2007; WAR YAR MEIN DA 2015].

 Text-reuse alignments computed by DharmaNexus show substantial shared material between the verses and the *Jātaka-aṭṭhakathā* as well as the *Cariyāpiṭaka-aṭṭhakathā*, alongside cross-language alignments with Āryaśūra’s Sanskrit *Jātakamālā* and Tibetan texts [DharmaNexus]. The legend also appears widely across Asian Buddhist literature and iconography, being preserved in Tibetan translation (*mkhas pa ri bon gi skyes rabs*), Thai cosmological literature (*Trai Phum Phra Ruang*), and ancient Japanese Buddhist art [Gaffney 2003; Jory 2016; Buddhist Virtues 2011].

**Parallels and text reuse**

- Text reuse within the Pali corpus (DharmaNexus): Jātaka-aṭṭhakathā (Tatiyo bhāgo) (Atk S0513a3) (§1.4–2.6 ↔ §411_1–415); Cariyāpiṭaka-aṭṭhakathā (Atk S0512a) (§1.4–3.4 ↔ §841_2–846)
- Cross-language matches (DharmaNexus): Āryaśūra: Jātakamālā (SA_T09_ajm_u) [sa]; རྟའི་ཚེའི་རིག་བྱེད་ཤ་ལི་ཧོ་ཏྲས་བསྡུས་པ་ཞེས་བྱ་བ། (śālihotrīyāśvāyurvedasaṃhitā-nāma) (D4345) [bo]
- [DharmaNexus] DharmaNexus text reuse and alignment database — Provided text reuse data with Pali commentaries and cross-language alignments with Sanskrit and Tibetan works.
- [Endo 1997] Toshiichi Endo, Buddha in Theravada Buddhism: A Study of the Concept of Buddha in the Pali Commentaries (1997) — Discussed the citation of Sasapaṇḍita in the Jātakanidānakathā and Buddhavaṃsa-aṭṭhakathā as an illustration of dānapāramī.
- [Buddhist Virtues 2011] 8th International Buddhist Conference, Buddhist Virtues in Socio-Economic Development (2011) — Identified the nipāta placement (Catukkanipāta, 316) and noted the tale's influence in Japanese Buddhist art.
- [Nyanaponika et al. 2003] Nyanaponika Thera, Hellmuth Hecker, and Bhikkhu Bodhi, Great Disciples of the Buddha (2003) — Summarized the narrative roles and past identities of Sāriputta, Moggallāna, Ānanda, and Sakka.
- [Ohnuma 2007] Reiko Ohnuma, Head, Eyes, Flesh and Blood: Giving Away the Body in Indian Buddhist Literature (2007) — Detailed the story of the present, the contrast of gifts, the dialogue, and the miraculous cooling of the fire.
- [Berkwitz 2006] Stephen C. Berkwitz, The History of the Buddha's Relic Shrine: A Translation of the Sinhala Thūpavaṃsa (2006) — Noted the Jātakaṭṭhakathā's citation of Ja 316 for the perfection of giving.
- [Gaffney 2003] Sean D. Gaffney, The Jātakanidānakathā: A Critical Study (2003) — Cited the Nidānakathā/Cariyāpiṭaka verse and corresponding Tibetan translation title.
- [Hazra 1994] Kanai Lal Hazra, Pāli Language and Literature (1994) — Documented the inclusion of the Sasapaṇḍita narrative in the Cariyāpiṭaka's dānapāramī section.
- [WAR YAR MEIN DA 2015] War Yar Mein Da, Pāramīs / Pāramitās in Theravada and Mahayana (2015) — Discussed the categorization of the hare's sacrifice as dāna-paramattha-pāramī and the placement of the hare image on the moon.
- [Jory 2016] Patrick Jory, Thailand's Theory of Monarchy: The Vessantara Jātaka and the Idea of the Perfect Man (2016) — Noted the presence of Sasapaṇḍita in the Thai Trai Phum Phra Ruang.
